passages.happening:
The book opens with its prophet. ‘These are the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests in Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin’ (verse 1).

The word of the LORD came to him in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (verse 2). It went on through the days of Jehoiakim, and ‘until the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah king of Judah, when the people of Jerusalem went into exile’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The heading dates Jeremiah's call to about 627 BC and runs his ministry to the summer of 587 or 586 BC, when Jerusalem fell and its people were taken to Babylon. That span covers the whole collapse of Judah.

Josiah, who reigned from about 640 to 609 BC, was a reforming king who tore down the shrines of other gods, especially after a book of the law was found in the temple in 622 BC. After his death his sons and a grandson reigned in quick succession, pressed first by Egypt and then by Babylon. The heading names only the three kings whose reigns were long enough to matter.

Anathoth was a village of priests in Benjamin, a few miles from Jerusalem. Jeremiah was a priest's son, so the man who would attack false trust in the temple grew up among its servants. The first hearers would know that the warnings came from inside.
passages.later: The book of Kings tells the same years, from Josiah's reform to the fall of the city (2 Kings 22 to 25). Ezra later says the return from exile came ‘to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah’ (Ezra 1:1).
passages.asks: Jeremiah's ministry ran through forty years of decline. Ask what it would take to keep speaking truth when nothing seemed to change. And ask what it means that God's word came to a real man in real years, under named kings.

passages.t: Known before birth, and too young to speak
passages.happening:
‘The word of the LORD came to me, saying’ (verse 4). God says, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (verse 5).

Jeremiah protests that he does not know how to speak, because he is only a child (verse 6). The LORD tells him not to say it. He must go to everyone God sends him to and speak all God commands (verse 7). ‘Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you’ (verse 8).

‘Then the LORD reached out His hand, touched my mouth’ (verse 9), and said he had put his words in Jeremiah's mouth. ‘See, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
The Hebrew word Jeremiah uses for child covers anyone from a baby to a young man not yet established, so he may have been a teenager or in his early twenties. In a culture that honored age, a young man had little standing to rebuke kings, priests and elders.

God's answer touches Jeremiah's mouth. Isaiah's lips were touched with a coal, and Deuteronomy had promised a prophet in whose mouth God would put his words. The first hearers would recognize the call of a true prophet.

The six verbs of verse 10 are the whole book in small. Four tear down and two build. Jeremiah's work would be mostly judgment, but it would end in building and planting.
passages.later: God had promised Moses, ‘I will put My words in his mouth’ (Deuteronomy 18:18). Paul uses words like these for his own call, saying God ‘set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by His grace’ (Galatians 1:15).
passages.hard:
Does verse 5 mean that God plans everything about every person's life before birth?

In its setting it is a particular word to Jeremiah about his calling as a prophet, not a general statement about every person's destiny. God knew him, set him apart and appointed him before he was born, which says that his calling came from God and not from himself. Theologians in the Reformed tradition see here God choosing a person for his purposes. Those in other traditions stress that Jeremiah still had to answer, protested, and later struggled bitterly with his call.

Many Christians also cite the verse, with Psalm 139:13-16, to say that God's relationship with a person begins before birth. That use draws a wider principle from a verse about a prophet's call, but it rests on something real in the text: God speaks of knowing Jeremiah in the womb as a person.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jeremiah said he was too young, and God said he was sent anyway. Ask what excuse you give for not doing what God has asked. And ask what it would mean for you to believe that God was with you to deliver you.

passages.t: An almond branch, a boiling pot, and an iron pillar
passages.happening:
God asks, Jeremiah, what do you see? Jeremiah sees a branch of an almond tree (verse 11). The LORD says he has seen correctly, ‘for I am watching over My word to accomplish it’ (verse 12).

Again God asks, and Jeremiah sees a boiling pot, tilting toward them from the north (verse 13). ‘Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land’ (verse 14). The kings of the north will set up their thrones at the gates of Jerusalem (verse 15). God will judge his people because they have forsaken him to burn incense to other gods (verse 16).

Jeremiah must get ready and speak, and not be terrified (verse 17). ‘Now behold, this day I have made you like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against the whole land’ (verse 18). They will fight against him but will not overcome him, since God is with him to deliver him (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The first vision depends on a pun. The almond was the first tree to blossom in Judah's late winter, and its Hebrew name, shaqed, sounds like the word for watching, shoqed. It was the waking tree. God is awake, watching over his word to do it.

The second vision draws on the map. Armies from Mesopotamia did not cross the Arabian desert. They followed the river valleys north and west and came down on Judah from the north. The pot boiling over from the north is an invading army.

Verse 18 turns a frightened young man into a fortified city. The whole land would be against him: kings, officials, priests and people. God does not promise that they will not fight him. He promises they will not win.
passages.later: God promised Joshua the same presence: ‘so will I be with you’ (Joshua 1:5). Jeremiah's later life tested the promise of verse 19: he was beaten, jailed and thrown into a cistern, yet not overcome (Jeremiah 38:13).
passages.asks: God says he is watching over his word to do it. Ask which of God's words you most need to know he is watching over. And ask where you are being asked to stand firm when everyone around is against you.
